title: The Daily Standup That Changes Decisions
summary: A standup where everyone updates but nothing gets decided has done half its job. How to end yours with a clear call: what finishes first, what waits, who helps whom.
author: Nguyen Le Phong
html:
Minute thirteen of standup. Everyone has given their update and people are reaching for their headphones. Then someone asks: "So are we still trying to finish the refund flow today?" Nobody answers right away. The ticket has been in review for three days, the one reviewer who knows that code is swamped, QA only has half the context, and an urgent request from sales is sitting near the top of the board.

That pause is the most useful moment of the whole meeting. Up to then, everyone has heard what everyone else is doing. Nobody has heard what the team decided. You can run a tidy fifteen-minute standup every day of the sprint and still walk out with the same fuzzy priorities you walked in with.

What the standup is actually for

The Scrum Guide is pretty clear on this. The Daily Scrum exists "to inspect progress toward the Sprint Goal and adapt the Sprint Backlog as necessary." The team can pick any format it likes, as long as the meeting focuses on progress toward the goal and ends with an actionable plan for the next day. The guide also says it promotes quick decision-making (The 2020 Scrum Guide). So by its own definition, a standup that inspects and never adapts has skipped half of its job.

Jason Yip's guide to stand-up patterns on Martin Fowler's site lists four goals: share understanding of goals, coordinate efforts, share problems and improvements, and identify as a team. Reporting status to a manager isn't on the list. He even names it as a smell, "Reporting to the Leader": people face the manager or facilitator and talk to them, when they should be talking to each other (Yip, It's Not Just Standing Up).

If your standup is still a round of "yesterday, today, blockers", start with the companion post on turning updates into a flow check. This one is about the step after that: once you can see the problem, make a call.

Ask what call would move the work

"Are you blocked?" is a weak question. Most people don't feel blocked, they feel slow, so the answer is "no, all good" and the ticket sits there another day. A stronger question is "what decision would get this moving?" The answer usually falls into one of three buckets:

  • A technical call: take the simpler implementation now and file the bigger refactor as its own ticket.
  • A product call: ship without the rare edge case behind a flag, or hold until someone understands it. Either is fine. Leaving it undecided for another day isn't.
  • A people call: ask for review right now, move a meeting so two people can pair, or say out loud that one person has five things in progress and needs to drop two.

Yip suggests a handy order for this: walk the board from the end of the process back to the start, so the items closest to done come up first. That makes the first decision of the day almost automatic: what are we finishing? Starting two fresh tickets feels productive. Getting one nearly-done ticket over the line actually is.

These calls feel too small to say out loud, and they're exactly what shapes the day. If nobody picks what finishes first, everyone defends their own plan. If nobody picks what can wait, the board fills with half-started work. If nobody picks who helps whom, people burn hours proving they can handle it alone. The team looks busy the whole time, and it pays interest on every half-finished ticket.

Three questions before everyone leaves

What do we finish first today? What can wait until tomorrow without hurting anyone? Who needs help, from whom, and by when? If the room can answer all three in a minute, the standup did its job.

The lead's job: name the trade-off, then step back

This part is tricky for leads. Decide everything yourself and the standup turns into a queue for permission. Avoid every decision and it turns into polite ambiguity, with everyone nodding and nothing settled. What works better sits in between: help the team name the trade-off, pick the smallest choice you can undo, and make one person the owner of the follow-up.

Most standup decisions are easy to undo. Jeff Bezos split decisions into two types in his 2015 letter to shareholders. Type 2 decisions are "changeable, reversible", two-way doors, and they "can and should be made quickly by high judgment individuals or small groups." He also warned that bigger organizations tend to run those through the heavy process meant for the irreversible ones, and the result is slowness (Amazon 2015 Letter to Shareholders). Which PR gets reviewed first, whether to pause a ticket, whether to pair for thirty minutes: all two-way doors. Make the call, look again tomorrow.

A standup isn't a problem-solving session, though. Yip's line for this is "Take It Offline": raise the issue in the standup, then let the two or three people who need to solve it stay on afterwards. The Scrum Guide says the same thing in its own words: developers often meet during the day to adapt or re-plan. The standup's output is the decision and the owner. The details can happen five minutes later.

When the team is running on empty

Decisions matter most when people are tired, and tired teams are the ones most likely to avoid them. Every option has a cost, so nobody wants to pick. Starting something new feels easier than asking why the old thing isn't done. "Let's sync later" feels safer than deciding who stops what they're doing.

A good standup takes some of that weight off. A vague "we're behind" breaks down into two or three honest choices the whole team makes together, so no single person ends up carrying the call alone. It's also a nicer way to start the morning than a round of updates that confirms what everyone already feared.

A one-line test

Here's the check I like: after standup, is at least one decision clearer than it was before? It doesn't have to be big. The team knows which PR gets reviewed first. A risky assumption goes to the product owner today instead of Friday. One ticket gets paused so another can finish. Someone leaves with an explicit "yes, ask for help now" instead of struggling for another afternoon.

If you want to make it visible, have whoever runs the standup post one line in the team channel afterwards: "Decided: finish refund flow first, sales request waits until tomorrow. Owner: Minh." It takes ten seconds, and anyone who missed the call knows where things stand.

Try this week

  • Walk the board right to left for one standup and see how many "finish this first" decisions come out of it.
  • Swap "are you blocked?" for "what decision would get this moving?" and listen for the answers.
  • End each standup with the three questions: what finishes first, what waits, who helps whom.
  • When a discussion runs long, name an owner and take it offline with only the people who need to be there.
  • Post the day's decision in one line in the team channel.

A standup doesn't need to impress anyone. It needs to make the day a little less accidental. When it changes even one small decision, the team chooses where its attention goes before the day chooses for it.

faqs.q: What is the purpose of a daily standup?
faqs.a: According to the 2020 Scrum Guide, the Daily Scrum is there to inspect progress toward the Sprint Goal and adapt the Sprint Backlog, ending with an actionable plan for the next day. Sharing updates is part of it. Changing the plan when the updates show a problem is the other half.

faqs.q: What questions should a team ask at standup?
faqs.a: Instead of only "are you blocked?", ask "what decision would get this moving?" Then close with three questions: what do we finish first today, what can wait, and who needs help from whom.

faqs.q: Should problems be solved during the standup?
faqs.a: No. Raise the issue, name an owner and a decision if you can, and let the two or three people who need to solve it stay on afterwards. Jason Yip calls this pattern "Take It Offline".

faqs.q: Should the team lead make the decisions at standup?
faqs.a: Mostly not. The lead helps the team name the trade-off, pick the smallest choice it can undo, and give one person the follow-up. Most standup decisions are reversible, the kind Jeff Bezos calls two-way doors, so they can be made quickly and revisited tomorrow.

faqs.q: How do I know if our standup is working?
faqs.a: After each standup, check whether at least one decision is clearer than before: which PR gets reviewed first, which ticket pauses, which risk goes to the product owner today. Posting that decision in one line in the team channel makes it easy to see.
